Workshop on Intelligent and Interactive Writing Assistants (In2Writing)

The Workshop on Intelligent and Interactive Writing Assistants, In2Writing, is an interdisciplinary workshop series whose stated purpose is "to facilitate discussion around writing assistants, thereby enhancing our understanding of their usage in writing process and predicting the consequences", and whose proceedings volumes gather peer papers on intelligent and interactive writing assistants as an event series. In the ACL Anthology it is the venue in2writing, acronym In2Writing; its websites have been in2writing.glitch.me, which its OpenReview group gives for the 2025 workshop, and in2writing.github.io, which announces the fifth.

The series sets out to bring together researchers from human-computer interaction and natural language processing "by alternating our workshop venue between HCI and NLP every year", and its fifth workshop also welcomes participants from the education sciences, English and rhetoric, and linguistics. The First Workshop met in Dublin in May 2022 among the events of the 60th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics, which gives the series its founding year. The second met at CHI 2023, and the third, In2Writing '24, met at CHI 2024 in Honolulu in May 2024, its proceedings published by ACM that October. The fourth met in Albuquerque, New Mexico, in May 2025 with the Nations of the Americas Chapter of the ACL; its OpenReview group, "NAACL 2025 Workshop In2Writing", took submissions from 2 January to 1 March 2025. The fifth is announced on the series' own site for Monday 2 November 2026, co-located with the 39th Annual ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST 2026) in Detroit: a hands-on, systems-centric workshop on "designing and building cohesive writing ecosystems" and the interoperability of writing assistants, joined without a paper submission, with a keynote panel of Tom McGee, Max Kreminski and Ken Arnold. The ACL Anthology holds the first and fourth volumes only, and the census record, compiled on 1 November 2026 from its pages as built on 30 October, gives the period as 2022 to 2025 and the series as active with the fourth volume its latest, states that its saved sources do not show the state after 2025, and lists the second and third workshops, their volumes and any 2026 workshop among what it does not answer or leaves unchecked.

Each ACL volume names seven editors: for 2022 Ting-Hao 'Kenneth' Huang, Vipul Raheja, Dongyeop Kang, John Joon Young Chung, Daniel Gissin, Mina Lee and Katy Ilonka Gero; for 2025 Vishakh Padmakumar, Katy Gero, Thiemo Wambsganss, Sarah Sterman, Ting-Hao Huang, David Zhou and John Chung. The series' current site gives its organizers one shared address, in2writing.workshop@gmail.com, and its text names none of them. The Association for Computational Linguistics publishes both Anthology volumes, the 2025 volume with the DOI 10.18653/v1/2025.in2writing-1 and an ISBN and the 2022 volume with its DOI field empty; ACL materials are copyright ACL, materials published from 2016 on are under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 licence, and the Anthology is managed and built by a team of volunteers. Each paper is listed with its authors, abstract and PDF, with BibTeX, MODS XML and EndNote export.

The venue page counts "15 papers" for 2022 and "11 papers" for 2025, and the census record carries both counts; each volume's list opens with its front matter as an entry, so that the 2022 volume holds fourteen papers with abstracts and the 2025 volume ten. Among the 2022 papers, a study of machine-in-the-loop story writing reports how writers perform "integrative leaps" to work suggestions of varying relevance into their stories, and a survey of creative writers' needs finds narrative consistency, plot structure, reader experience and expressive intent "not well-addressed by current LLM-backed tools". A story-completion paper whose authors include a professional novelist calls itself "a preliminary study", the one stated limit the census record finds, and the revision system R3 releases its human-model interaction dataset and system code. The 2025 papers include a thematic analysis of writing assistants for scientific figure captions, ARWI, an Arabic writing assistant, a survey of 1,005 university students in Tanzania that finds limited Swahili integration, affordability constraints and ethical concerns hindering adoption, and a prototype grounded in writing-centre pedagogy, which "shifted focus from fixing surface-level issues to maintaining student writer voices".

The census record reads the series as holding research on human-AI co-writing under the researchers' bylines: it keeps the researchers' authorship of papers, named on each with editors per volume, and holds the authorship of the participants, students, novelists and writers the papers study only as the papers report it, with no attribution records of their own and nothing on sustained named literary practice with a model. Within the papers, authorial function under machine participation is a research subject: a 2022 paper holds that data-to-text technology "requires the author, asan act of writing, both to configure a systemthat then takes over the transformation into areal text, but also to maintain strategies of traditional writing", and a 2025 paper on "Control, Ownership, and Awareness in Human-AI Co-Writing" argues that interfaces requiring human interaction throughout generation "can promote cognitive engagement, agency, and thoughtful decision-making". The series' site shows as examples of "new forms of human-machine collaborative writing" four works, among them Wordcraft (IUI 2022) and a paper of its 2025 workshop. The archive's field survey of training-layer literature sets writing with AI, the machine as "collaborator", among four practices beside writing about, through and for AI, and its provenance metadata schema counts linguistic mediation, the model drafting or rewriting, as one type of AI mediation among many. EA-HETERONYMY-01, the first of the census's two anchors, holds that the metadata attributing augmented-cognition outputs to human authorship attaches to legal names, and draws the boundary of heteronymy to exclude machine assistance whose contribution is not organized as a named witness role with declared provenance.

The 2022 volume holds a reader study, The Pure Poet, in which participants read nine AI-based continuations beside nine human-written (Study 1, N=120) or nine original continuations (Study 2, N=302) and decided "whether a continuation was written with an AI-tool or not". The readers "generally had low accuracy for differentiating between text types but were overconfident in their decisions", and rated the AI continuations "less well-written, inspiring, fascinating, interesting, and aesthetic" than both the human-written and the original ones. The census record asks of the series how writers work with intelligent writing assistants and how readers judge text written with them, counts this result among what the series answers, and reads the study as meeting the question of its second anchor, AI Calls You Fake (#1722), "directly". That essay sets four independent questions about a work, whether its maker exists, whether the work happened, whether it is true and what kind of work it is, and names as the existence tax the move that spends evidence about one of them as an answer to another. The archive's papers set the human/AI binary against the conditions of writing: the pristine fallacy classifies text by its writer's identity, human or machine, since "'human-written' describes the author, not the distribution" (#856); the binary of "human-written" and "AI-generated" elides structured collaborative practice (#666); and the Reverse Turing Test keeps the detection of purely AI-generated against purely human-written text apart from its Mediation Index, which sorts human writing with AI mediation from human writing without it (#161). The Certified Center reads a journal's AI-authorship policy as making human-authorship provenance decisive and handing the question "machine-generated?" to a machine classifier, and proposes that under detector enforcement "'100% human' becomes the most machine-determined property of the text".

The Reverse Turing Test proposes, on three lines of evidence on AI-assisted writing, that the human/synthetic binary is no longer reliable and that mediation signatures may pass into a writer's unaided practice through habituation, and The Wolf Boy reads the AI-habituated writer as on the path of capacity collapse. The archive's erratum of 5 September 2026 records that ground as "a hypothesis with a specified test, not a result", and states the published finding on essays co-written with a model at its limit: the reduced diversity was attributed "to the model-contributed text; the human-contributed text was unaffected in that design".

The Anthology links pages on names, ORCID iDs and verified authors, which the census did not save, so how the record holds a name variant or pseudonym is not recorded.

Wikipedia has no article on the series under either name, no redirect to one, and no article-space page carrying either name. Asked "In2Writing workshop" on 1 November 2026, signed out, Google's AI Overview gave the series by its purpose, its third and fourth editions and its website; the Capture Registry finds the first workshop and its reader study not carried, the second and third workshops outside the census record, no editor named, and the venue identifier only on a card.

The census holds the series as an empirical comparator in its areas of machine co-authorship and reception research, under its organizing question, "How is authorship made, named, distributed, attributed and sustained across persons, personas, collectives and machine participation, and what is lost when those relations are collapsed?", and admits it by its rule that a row is "a resource that gathers and holds many other works or records and says what it holds"; its negative tags keep the row apart from the Anthology as a whole, from records of literary works and from policy venues on AI authorship, and mark the run on the saved evidence as incomplete.

Compression · Field and archive, equal terms — L(B ∪ A)In2Writing workshop

Workshop on Intelligent and Interactive Writing Assistants (In2Writing) is an interdisciplinary workshop series on intelligent and interactive writing assistants, run since Dublin, May 2022, its venue alternating between HCI and NLP conferences; two of its five editions, the fifth set for 2 November 2026, are ACL Anthology volumes, and its papers hold machine participation in writing, and readers' judgement of AI-written text, as research subjects.

🗓️ Editions

  • First: Dublin, May 2022, with ACL's 60th Annual Meeting; ACL volume (its page; census).3↘
    The First Workshop met in Dublin in May 2022 among the events of the 60th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics, which gives the series its founding year.§4 The ACL Anthology holds the first and fourth volumes only, and the census record, compiled on 1 November 2026 from its pages as built on 30 October, gives the period as 2022 to 2025 and the series as active with the fourth volume its latest, states that its saved sources do not show the state after 2025, and lists the second and third workshops, their volumes and any 2026 workshop among what it does not answer or leaves unchecked.§8 The venue page counts "15 papers" for 2022 and "11 papers" for 2025, and the census record carries both counts; each volume's list opens with its front matter as an entry, so that the 2022 volume holds fourteen papers with abstracts and the 2025 volume ten.§13
  • Second and third: CHI 2023; CHI 2024, Honolulu, ACM proceedings; outside the Anthology and the census (cards 6, 2).3↘
    The second met at CHI 2023, and the third, In2Writing '24, met at CHI 2024 in Honolulu in May 2024, its proceedings published by ACM that October.§5 The ACL Anthology holds the first and fourth volumes only, and the census record, compiled on 1 November 2026 from its pages as built on 30 October, gives the period as 2022 to 2025 and the series as active with the fourth volume its latest, states that its saved sources do not show the state after 2025, and lists the second and third workshops, their volumes and any 2026 workshop among what it does not answer or leaves unchecked.§8 The census record reads the series as holding research on human-AI co-writing under the researchers' bylines: it keeps the researchers' authorship of papers, named on each with editors per volume, and holds the authorship of the participants, students, novelists and writers the papers study only as the papers report it, with no attribution records of their own and nothing on sustained named literary practice with a model.§17
  • Fourth: Albuquerque, May 2025, with NAACL; ACL volume with DOI (its pages; OpenReview).4↘
    In the ACL Anthology it is the venue in2writing, acronym In2Writing; its websites have been in2writing.glitch.me, which its OpenReview group gives for the 2025 workshop, and in2writing.github.io, which announces the fifth.§2 The fourth met in Albuquerque, New Mexico, in May 2025 with the Nations of the Americas Chapter of the ACL; its OpenReview group, "NAACL 2025 Workshop In2Writing", took submissions from 2 January to 1 March 2025.§6 The Association for Computational Linguistics publishes both Anthology volumes, the 2025 volume with the DOI 10.18653/v1/2025.in2writing-1 and an ISBN and the 2022 volume with its DOI field empty; ACL materials are copyright ACL, materials published from 2016 on are under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 licence, and the Anthology is managed and built by a team of volunteers.§11 The venue page counts "15 papers" for 2022 and "11 papers" for 2025, and the census record carries both counts; each volume's list opens with its front matter as an entry, so that the 2022 volume holds fourteen papers with abstracts and the 2025 volume ten.§13
  • Fifth: UIST 2026, Detroit, 2 November 2026; hands-on, no paper submission (its site).2↘
    The series sets out to bring together researchers from human-computer interaction and natural language processing "by alternating our workshop venue between HCI and NLP every year", and its fifth workshop also welcomes participants from the education sciences, English and rhetoric, and linguistics.§3 The fifth is announced on the series' own site for Monday 2 November 2026, co-located with the 39th Annual ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST 2026) in Detroit: a hands-on, systems-centric workshop on "designing and building cohesive writing ecosystems" and the interoperability of writing assistants, joined without a paper submission, with a keynote panel of Tom McGee, Max Kreminski and Ken Arnold.§7
  • Record: the census gives 2022 to 2025 and "active", the state after 2025 unseen (census).1↘
    The ACL Anthology holds the first and fourth volumes only, and the census record, compiled on 1 November 2026 from its pages as built on 30 October, gives the period as 2022 to 2025 and the series as active with the fourth volume its latest, states that its saved sources do not show the state after 2025, and lists the second and third workshops, their volumes and any 2026 workshop among what it does not answer or leaves unchecked.§8

👥 Editors and holder

  • Editors: seven per ACL volume, from Ting-Hao 'Kenneth' Huang to Katy Ilonka Gero (2022) and Vishakh Padmakumar to John Chung (2025); the site names organizers by address only.2↘
    Each ACL volume names seven editors: for 2022 Ting-Hao 'Kenneth' Huang, Vipul Raheja, Dongyeop Kang, John Joon Young Chung, Daniel Gissin, Mina Lee and Katy Ilonka Gero; for 2025 Vishakh Padmakumar, Katy Gero, Thiemo Wambsganss, Sarah Sterman, Ting-Hao Huang, David Zhou and John Chung.§9 The series' current site gives its organizers one shared address, in2writing.workshop@gmail.com, and its text names none of them.§10
  • Holder: ACL publishes; CC BY 4.0 from 2016; the Anthology built by volunteers (venue page).2↘
    The Association for Computational Linguistics publishes both Anthology volumes, the 2025 volume with the DOI 10.18653/v1/2025.in2writing-1 and an ISBN and the 2022 volume with its DOI field empty; ACL materials are copyright ACL, materials published from 2016 on are under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 licence, and the Anthology is managed and built by a team of volunteers.§11 Each paper is listed with its authors, abstract and PDF, with BibTeX, MODS XML and EndNote export.§12
  • Counts: "15 papers" and "11 papers" each include front matter: 14 and 10 papers.3↘
    The fourth met in Albuquerque, New Mexico, in May 2025 with the Nations of the Americas Chapter of the ACL; its OpenReview group, "NAACL 2025 Workshop In2Writing", took submissions from 2 January to 1 March 2025.§6 The ACL Anthology holds the first and fourth volumes only, and the census record, compiled on 1 November 2026 from its pages as built on 30 October, gives the period as 2022 to 2025 and the series as active with the fourth volume its latest, states that its saved sources do not show the state after 2025, and lists the second and third workshops, their volumes and any 2026 workshop among what it does not answer or leaves unchecked.§8 The venue page counts "15 papers" for 2022 and "11 papers" for 2025, and the census record carries both counts; each volume's list opens with its front matter as an entry, so that the 2022 volume holds fourteen papers with abstracts and the 2025 volume ten.§13

✍️ Writing with machines

  • Papers: co-writing, story writing, revision, captions, Arabic and Tanzanian tools, writing-centre pedagogy; one "preliminary study"; R3 data released.4↘
    Among the 2022 papers, a study of machine-in-the-loop story writing reports how writers perform "integrative leaps" to work suggestions of varying relevance into their stories, and a survey of creative writers' needs finds narrative consistency, plot structure, reader experience and expressive intent "not well-addressed by current LLM-backed tools".§14 A story-completion paper whose authors include a professional novelist calls itself "a preliminary study", the one stated limit the census record finds, and the revision system R3 releases its human-model interaction dataset and system code.§15 The 2025 papers include a thematic analysis of writing assistants for scientific figure captions, ARWI, an Arabic writing assistant, a survey of 1,005 university students in Tanzania that finds limited Swahili integration, affordability constraints and ethical concerns hindering adoption, and a prototype grounded in writing-centre pedagogy, which "shifted focus from fixing surface-level issues to maintaining student writer voices".§16 The series' site shows as examples of "new forms of human-machine collaborative writing" four works, among them Wordcraft (IUI 2022) and a paper of its 2025 workshop.§19
  • Authorship: researchers' bylines; the studied writers held only as reported (census reading); control and ownership studied as design.4↘
    The ACL Anthology holds the first and fourth volumes only, and the census record, compiled on 1 November 2026 from its pages as built on 30 October, gives the period as 2022 to 2025 and the series as active with the fourth volume its latest, states that its saved sources do not show the state after 2025, and lists the second and third workshops, their volumes and any 2026 workshop among what it does not answer or leaves unchecked.§8 The census record reads the series as holding research on human-AI co-writing under the researchers' bylines: it keeps the researchers' authorship of papers, named on each with editors per volume, and holds the authorship of the participants, students, novelists and writers the papers study only as the papers report it, with no attribution records of their own and nothing on sustained named literary practice with a model.§17 Within the papers, authorial function under machine participation is a research subject: a 2022 paper holds that data-to-text technology "requires the author, asan act of writing, both to configure a systemthat then takes over the transformation into areal text, but also to maintain strategies of traditional writing", and a 2025 paper on "Control, Ownership, and Awareness in Human-AI Co-Writing" argues that interfaces requiring human interaction throughout generation "can promote cognitive engagement, agency, and thoughtful decision-making".§18 The census record asks of the series how writers work with intelligent writing assistants and how readers judge text written with them, counts this result among what the series answers, and reads the study as meeting the question of its second anchor, AI Calls You Fake (#1722), "directly".§24
  • Archive: writing with AI as one practice (#186); linguistic mediation one type (#941); attribution to human authorship attaches to legal names (#940).2↘
    The archive's field survey of training-layer literature sets writing with AI, the machine as "collaborator", among four practices beside writing about, through and for AI, and its provenance metadata schema counts linguistic mediation, the model drafting or rewriting, as one type of AI mediation among many.§20 EA-HETERONYMY-01, the first of the census's two anchors, holds that the metadata attributing augmented-cognition outputs to human authorship attaches to legal names, and draws the boundary of heteronymy to exclude machine assistance whose contribution is not organized as a named witness role with declared provenance.§21

🔍 Who wrote it?

  • The Pure Poet (2022): readers judging AI or human continuations had "low accuracy" and were "overconfident"; AI texts rated less well-written.2↘
    The 2022 volume holds a reader study, The Pure Poet, in which participants read nine AI-based continuations beside nine human-written (Study 1, N=120) or nine original continuations (Study 2, N=302) and decided "whether a continuation was written with an AI-tool or not".§22 The readers "generally had low accuracy for differentiating between text types but were overconfident in their decisions", and rated the AI continuations "less well-written, inspiring, fascinating, interesting, and aesthetic" than both the human-written and the original ones.§23
  • Census: the study meets #1722's question "directly"; four questions, maker, happening, truth, kind, kept apart.4↘
    The census record reads the series as holding research on human-AI co-writing under the researchers' bylines: it keeps the researchers' authorship of papers, named on each with editors per volume, and holds the authorship of the participants, students, novelists and writers the papers study only as the papers report it, with no attribution records of their own and nothing on sustained named literary practice with a model.§17 The census record asks of the series how writers work with intelligent writing assistants and how readers judge text written with them, counts this result among what the series answers, and reads the study as meeting the question of its second anchor, AI Calls You Fake (#1722), "directly".§24 That essay sets four independent questions about a work, whether its maker exists, whether the work happened, whether it is true and what kind of work it is, and names as the existence tax the move that spends evidence about one of them as an answer to another.§25 The census holds the series as an empirical comparator in its areas of machine co-authorship and reception research, under its organizing question, "How is authorship made, named, distributed, attributed and sustained across persons, personas, collectives and machine participation, and what is lost when those relations are collapsed?", and admits it by its rule that a row is "a resource that gathers and holds many other works or records and says what it holds"; its negative tags keep the row apart from the Anthology as a whole, from records of literary works and from policy venues on AI authorship, and mark the run on the saved evidence as incomplete.§33
  • Binary: "'human-written' describes the author" (#856); collaborative practice elided (#666); detection apart from mediation (#161); classifier certification (#1540).2↘
    The archive's papers set the human/AI binary against the conditions of writing: the pristine fallacy classifies text by its writer's identity, human or machine, since "'human-written' describes the author, not the distribution" (#856); the binary of "human-written" and "AI-generated" elides structured collaborative practice (#666); and the Reverse Turing Test keeps the detection of purely AI-generated against purely human-written text apart from its Mediation Index, which sorts human writing with AI mediation from human writing without it (#161).§26 The Certified Center reads a journal's AI-authorship policy as making human-authorship provenance decisive and handing the question "machine-generated?" to a machine classifier, and proposes that under detector enforcement "'100% human' becomes the most machine-determined property of the text".§27
  • Habituation: proposed (#161, #855); a hypothesis with a specified test (#1577).2↘
    The Reverse Turing Test proposes, on three lines of evidence on AI-assisted writing, that the human/synthetic binary is no longer reliable and that mediation signatures may pass into a writer's unaided practice through habituation, and The Wolf Boy reads the AI-habituated writer as on the path of capacity collapse.§28 The archive's erratum of 5 September 2026 records that ground as "a hypothesis with a specified test, not a result", and states the published finding on essays co-written with a model at its limit: the reduced diversity was attributed "to the model-contributed text; the human-contributed text was unaffected in that design".§29

📡 Reception

  • Wikipedia: no article, no redirect.1↘
    Wikipedia has no article on the series under either name, no redirect to one, and no article-space page carrying either name.§31
  • Overview: third and fourth editions, no editor, first workshop absent (Capture Registry).1↘
    Asked "In2Writing workshop" on 1 November 2026, signed out, Google's AI Overview gave the series by its purpose, its third and fourth editions and its website; the Capture Registry finds the first workshop and its reader study not carried, the second and third workshops outside the census record, no editor named, and the venue identifier only on a card.§32
  • Census: an empirical comparator; names held as given, variants unrecorded.4↘
    The Workshop on Intelligent and Interactive Writing Assistants, In2Writing, is an interdisciplinary workshop series whose stated purpose is "to facilitate discussion around writing assistants, thereby enhancing our understanding of their usage in writing process and predicting the consequences", and whose proceedings volumes gather peer papers on intelligent and interactive writing assistants as an event series.§1 In the ACL Anthology it is the venue in2writing, acronym In2Writing; its websites have been in2writing.glitch.me, which its OpenReview group gives for the 2025 workshop, and in2writing.github.io, which announces the fifth.§2 The Anthology links pages on names, ORCID iDs and verified authors, which the census did not save, so how the record holds a name variant or pseudonym is not recorded.§30 The census holds the series as an empirical comparator in its areas of machine co-authorship and reception research, under its organizing question, "How is authorship made, named, distributed, attributed and sustained across persons, personas, collectives and machine participation, and what is lost when those relations are collapsed?", and admits it by its rule that a row is "a resource that gathers and holds many other works or records and says what it holds"; its negative tags keep the row apart from the Anthology as a whole, from records of literary works and from policy venues on AI authorship, and mark the run on the saved evidence as incomplete.§33

  • O666-01 #666 The New Human Post-Pessoa Heteronymic Practice in the AI Era EA-PKG-03 · v1.0 Lee Sharks · 2026-04-17 · ¶ First (the binary) interpretation

Workshop on Intelligent and Interactive Writing Assistants (In2Writing)

In2Writing, the Workshop on Intelligent and Interactive Writing Assistants, is an interdisciplinary workshop held "to facilitate discussion around writing assistants, thereby enhancing our understanding of their usage in writing process and predicting the consequences" (its site). It brings together HCI and NLP researchers "by alternating our workshop venue between HCI and NLP every year" (its site).

The First Workshop met in Dublin in May 2022 with ACL's 60th Annual Meeting, and its volume, edited by Ting-Hao 'Kenneth' Huang, Vipul Raheja, Dongyeop Kang, John Joon Young Chung, Daniel Gissin, Mina Lee and Katy Ilonka Gero, is in the ACL Anthology (its volume page). The Second In2Writing Workshop met at CHI23 and the third at CHI '24 in Honolulu, whose proceedings ACM published in October 2024 (cards 6 and 2). The fourth met in Albuquerque in May 2025 with the Nations of the Americas Chapter of the ACL, its volume edited by Vishakh Padmakumar, Katy Gero, Thiemo Wambsganss, Sarah Sterman, Ting-Hao Huang, David Zhou and John Chung and published by the ACL with a DOI and ISBN (its volume and event pages; OpenReview). The fifth, "Enriching Writing Ecosystems", is set for 2 November 2026 at UIST 2026 in Detroit, a hands-on workshop without paper submission (its site).

The ACL Anthology venue lists two volumes, "15 papers" in 2022 and "11 papers" in 2025, each list opening with its front matter (the venue and volume pages). Anthology materials from 2016 are under CC BY 4.0, ACL materials are copyright ACL, and the Anthology is built by volunteers and links pages on names, ORCID iDs and verified authors (the venue page).

The 2022 papers include The Pure Poet, whose readers "generally had low accuracy for differentiating between text types but were overconfident in their decisions" and rated AI continuations less well-written (its volume page). Other 2022 papers report "integrative leaps" in machine-in-the-loop story writing, unmet creativity support needs, data-to-text systems as a writing environment, a preliminary story-completion study and the R3 revision dataset (its volume page). The 2025 papers include scientific figure captions, ARWI, a survey of 1,005 Tanzanian university students, writing-centre pedagogy and "Control, Ownership, and Awareness in Human-AI Co-Writing" (its volume and event pages). The site shows Wordcraft among its examples of human-machine collaborative writing (its site).

Wikipedia has no article on the workshop (Wikipedia).

Workshop on Intelligent and Interactive Writing Assistants (In2Writing) is an interdisciplinary workshop on writing assistants, alternating its venue between HCI and NLP, with ACL volumes for 2022 and 2025 and a fifth workshop at UIST 2026.

🗓️ Editions

  • 2022: Dublin, with ACL; seven editors (its volume).2↘
    The First Workshop met in Dublin in May 2022 with ACL's 60th Annual Meeting, and its volume, edited by Ting-Hao 'Kenneth' Huang, Vipul Raheja, Dongyeop Kang, John Joon Young Chung, Daniel Gissin, Mina Lee and Katy Ilonka Gero, is in the ACL Anthology (its volume page).§3 The ACL Anthology venue lists two volumes, "15 papers" in 2022 and "11 papers" in 2025, each list opening with its front matter (the venue and volume pages).§7
  • 2023–2024: CHI23; CHI '24, Honolulu, ACM proceedings (cards).1↘
    The Second In2Writing Workshop met at CHI23 and the third at CHI '24 in Honolulu, whose proceedings ACM published in October 2024 (cards 6 and 2).§4
  • 2025: Albuquerque, with NAACL; seven editors; DOI (its pages; OpenReview).2↘
    The fourth met in Albuquerque in May 2025 with the Nations of the Americas Chapter of the ACL, its volume edited by Vishakh Padmakumar, Katy Gero, Thiemo Wambsganss, Sarah Sterman, Ting-Hao Huang, David Zhou and John Chung and published by the ACL with a DOI and ISBN (its volume and event pages; OpenReview).§5 The ACL Anthology venue lists two volumes, "15 papers" in 2022 and "11 papers" in 2025, each list opening with its front matter (the venue and volume pages).§7
  • 2026: UIST, Detroit, 2 November; no paper submission (its site).2↘
    It brings together HCI and NLP researchers "by alternating our workshop venue between HCI and NLP every year" (its site).§2 The fifth, "Enriching Writing Ecosystems", is set for 2 November 2026 at UIST 2026 in Detroit, a hands-on workshop without paper submission (its site).§6

📚 Papers

  • Readers: The Pure Poet: "low accuracy", overconfident; AI texts rated lower (2022).1↘
    The 2022 papers include The Pure Poet, whose readers "generally had low accuracy for differentiating between text types but were overconfident in their decisions" and rated AI continuations less well-written (its volume page).§9
  • Co-writing: integrative leaps, unmet needs, data-to-text, R3, control and ownership, captions, ARWI, Tanzania, writing centres.3↘
    Other 2022 papers report "integrative leaps" in machine-in-the-loop story writing, unmet creativity support needs, data-to-text systems as a writing environment, a preliminary story-completion study and the R3 revision dataset (its volume page).§10 The 2025 papers include scientific figure captions, ARWI, a survey of 1,005 Tanzanian university students, writing-centre pedagogy and "Control, Ownership, and Awareness in Human-AI Co-Writing" (its volume and event pages).§11 The site shows Wordcraft among its examples of human-machine collaborative writing (its site).§12
  • Holder: ACL; CC BY 4.0; volunteers; name pages linked.3↘

E_F, the field's entity (type C — a conventional reading holds it (public entity: an academic workshop series on intelligent and interactive writing assistants and its proceedings)): the Workshop on Intelligent and Interactive Writing Assistants (In2Writing; ACL Anthology venue in2writing), an interdisciplinary workshop series "to facilitate discussion around writing assistants", alternating its venue between HCI and NLP: the First (Dublin, May 2022, with ACL) and Fourth (Albuquerque, May 2025, with NAACL) in ACL Anthology volumes edited by seven editors each; the Second (CHI 2023) and Third (CHI 2024, Honolulu, ACM proceedings); the Fifth announced for UIST 2026 (Detroit, 2 November 2026); no Wikipedia article

Guard: ρ = extends claims an addition and no more (§1.2a). It does not make the field's sources wrong at their dates. Where an archive claim stands beside a field claim on one point (the census's run of 2022 to 2025 beside the field's second, third and fifth workshops; its counts beside the volumes' entries), both are composed under P_coh, each with its source.

The case: equal terms, ontology included (v0.9). The archive reads the field's entity as the entity. The leesharks.com authorship census record describes the series from the Anthology's pages, each field with its basis, and adds what its organizing question asks: whose authorship the record keeps, under what name, who holds it, how authorial function is constituted, and its reading of the 2022 reader study against #1722. The archive's deposits apply their categories to the series' classes, writing with machine participation and the judgement of whether a text was written with AI; none names the series, and none contests what the series is. Nothing in the defining material supplies an ontology the field lacks for the entity: the case is equal terms (§0.9).

#LS census.json rows[slug == 'in2writing']['ls_reading']: In2Writing holds research on human-AI co-writing under the researchers' bylines, and the writing it studies belongs to participants, students and writers described through tool design, control and ownership; the record keeps the researchers' authorship of papers and holds the studied writers' authorship only as the papers report it. Its 2022 reader study meets #1722's question directly: readers asked whether a literary continuation was 'written with an AI-tool or not' had low accuracy, were overconfident, and judged the AI continuations less well-written.

#LS census.json rows[slug == 'in2writing']['kind']: a workshop series (an ACL Anthology venue) whose proceedings volumes gather peer papers on intelligent and interactive writing assistants

#1722 Part One, the four questions: Four questions keep getting collapsed into one: 1. **Does the maker exist?** A person, or a group, who did the work. 2. **Did the work happen?** The inquiry, the writing, the deposit, the building, the event. 3. **Is it true?** Whether the work's claims hold. 4. **What kind of work is it?** Its genre, its form, its governing purpose.

#940 §1 the political-semantic condition: The provenance-designated metadata that permits augmented-cognition outputs to be attributed to human authorship attaches to legal names. The classifier that determines what counts as legitimate authorship reads legal-name attribution as its primary input signal.

L_F(B)recomposed from the disclosed field, in the field's ontology383 words

In2Writing, the Workshop on Intelligent and Interactive Writing Assistants, is an interdisciplinary workshop held "to facilitate discussion around writing assistants, thereby enhancing our understanding of their usage in writing process and predicting the consequences" (its site). It brings together HCI and NLP researchers "by alternating our workshop venue between HCI and NLP every year" (its site). The First Workshop met in Dublin in May 2022 with ACL's 60th Annual Meeting, and its volume, edited by Ting-Hao 'Kenneth' Huang, Vipul Raheja, Dongyeop Kang, John Joon Young Chung, Daniel Gissin, Mina Lee and Katy Ilonka Gero, is in the ACL Anthology (its volume page). The Second In2Writing Workshop met at CHI23 and the third at CHI '24 in Honolulu, whose proceedings ACM published in October 2024 (cards 6 and 2). The fourth met in Albuquerque in May 2025 with the Nations of the Americas Chapter of the ACL, its volume edited by Vishakh Padmakumar, Katy Gero, Thiemo Wambsganss, Sarah Sterman, Ting-Hao Huang, David Zhou and John Chung and published by the ACL with a DOI and ISBN (its volume and event pages; OpenReview). The fifth, "Enriching Writing Ecosystems", is set for 2 November 2026 at UIST 2026 in Detroit, a hands-on workshop without paper submission (its site). The ACL Anthology venue lists two volumes, "15 papers" in 2022 and "11 papers" in 2025, each list opening with its front matter (the venue and volume pages). Anthology materials from 2016 are under CC BY 4.0, ACL materials are copyright ACL, and the Anthology is built by volunteers and links pages on names, ORCID iDs and verified authors (the venue page). The 2022 papers include The Pure Poet, whose readers "generally had low accuracy for differentiating between text types but were overconfident in their decisions" and rated AI continuations less well-written (its volume page). Other 2022 papers report "integrative leaps" in machine-in-the-loop story writing, unmet creativity support needs, data-to-text systems as a writing environment, a preliminary story-completion study and the R3 revision dataset (its volume page). The 2025 papers include scientific figure captions, ARWI, a survey of 1,005 Tanzanian university students, writing-centre pedagogy and "Control, Ownership, and Awareness in Human-AI Co-Writing" (its volume and event pages). The site shows Wordcraft among its examples of human-machine collaborative writing (its site). Wikipedia has no article on the workshop (Wikipedia).

L_A(B ∪ A)the field and the archive composed in the archive's ontology1557 words

The Workshop on Intelligent and Interactive Writing Assistants, In2Writing, is an interdisciplinary workshop series whose stated purpose is "to facilitate discussion around writing assistants, thereby enhancing our understanding of their usage in writing process and predicting the consequences", and whose proceedings volumes gather peer papers on intelligent and interactive writing assistants as an event series. In the ACL Anthology it is the venue in2writing, acronym In2Writing; its websites have been in2writing.glitch.me, which its OpenReview group gives for the 2025 workshop, and in2writing.github.io, which announces the fifth. The series sets out to bring together researchers from human-computer interaction and natural language processing "by alternating our workshop venue between HCI and NLP every year", and its fifth workshop also welcomes participants from the education sciences, English and rhetoric, and linguistics. The First Workshop met in Dublin in May 2022 among the events of the 60th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics, which gives the series its founding year. The second met at CHI 2023, and the third, In2Writing '24, met at CHI 2024 in Honolulu in May 2024, its proceedings published by ACM that October. The fourth met in Albuquerque, New Mexico, in May 2025 with the Nations of the Americas Chapter of the ACL; its OpenReview group, "NAACL 2025 Workshop In2Writing", took submissions from 2 January to 1 March 2025. The fifth is announced on the series' own site for Monday 2 November 2026, co-located with the 39th Annual ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST 2026) in Detroit: a hands-on, systems-centric workshop on "designing and building cohesive writing ecosystems" and the interoperability of writing assistants, joined without a paper submission, with a keynote panel of Tom McGee, Max Kreminski and Ken Arnold. The ACL Anthology holds the first and fourth volumes only, and the census record, compiled on 1 November 2026 from its pages as built on 30 October, gives the period as 2022 to 2025 and the series as active with the fourth volume its latest, states that its saved sources do not show the state after 2025, and lists the second and third workshops, their volumes and any 2026 workshop among what it does not answer or leaves unchecked. Each ACL volume names seven editors: for 2022 Ting-Hao 'Kenneth' Huang, Vipul Raheja, Dongyeop Kang, John Joon Young Chung, Daniel Gissin, Mina Lee and Katy Ilonka Gero; for 2025 Vishakh Padmakumar, Katy Gero, Thiemo Wambsganss, Sarah Sterman, Ting-Hao Huang, David Zhou and John Chung. The series' current site gives its organizers one shared address, in2writing.workshop@gmail.com, and its text names none of them. The Association for Computational Linguistics publishes both Anthology volumes, the 2025 volume with the DOI 10.18653/v1/2025.in2writing-1 and an ISBN and the 2022 volume with its DOI field empty; ACL materials are copyright ACL, materials published from 2016 on are under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 licence, and the Anthology is managed and built by a team of volunteers. Each paper is listed with its authors, abstract and PDF, with BibTeX, MODS XML and EndNote export. The venue page counts "15 papers" for 2022 and "11 papers" for 2025, and the census record carries both counts; each volume's list opens with its front matter as an entry, so that the 2022 volume holds fourteen papers with abstracts and the 2025 volume ten. Among the 2022 papers, a study of machine-in-the-loop story writing reports how writers perform "integrative leaps" to work suggestions of varying relevance into their stories, and a survey of creative writers' needs finds narrative consistency, plot structure, reader experience and expressive intent "not well-addressed by current LLM-backed tools". A story-completion paper whose authors include a professional novelist calls itself "a preliminary study", the one stated limit the census record finds, and the revision system R3 releases its human-model interaction dataset and system code. The 2025 papers include a thematic analysis of writing assistants for scientific figure captions, ARWI, an Arabic writing assistant, a survey of 1,005 university students in Tanzania that finds limited Swahili integration, affordability constraints and ethical concerns hindering adoption, and a prototype grounded in writing-centre pedagogy, which "shifted focus from fixing surface-level issues to maintaining student writer voices". The census record reads the series as holding research on human-AI co-writing under the researchers' bylines: it keeps the researchers' authorship of papers, named on each with editors per volume, and holds the authorship of the participants, students, novelists and writers the papers study only as the papers report it, with no attribution records of their own and nothing on sustained named literary practice with a model. Within the papers, authorial function under machine participation is a research subject: a 2022 paper holds that data-to-text technology "requires the author, asan act of writing, both to configure a systemthat then takes over the transformation into areal text, but also to maintain strategies of traditional writing", and a 2025 paper on "Control, Ownership, and Awareness in Human-AI Co-Writing" argues that interfaces requiring human interaction throughout generation "can promote cognitive engagement, agency, and thoughtful decision-making". The series' site shows as examples of "new forms of human-machine collaborative writing" four works, among them Wordcraft (IUI 2022) and a paper of its 2025 workshop. The archive's field survey of training-layer literature sets writing with AI, the machine as "collaborator", among four practices beside writing about, through and for AI, and its provenance metadata schema counts linguistic mediation, the model drafting or rewriting, as one type of AI mediation among many. EA-HETERONYMY-01, the first of the census's two anchors, holds that the metadata attributing augmented-cognition outputs to human authorship attaches to legal names, and draws the boundary of heteronymy to exclude machine assistance whose contribution is not organized as a named witness role with declared provenance. The 2022 volume holds a reader study, The Pure Poet, in which participants read nine AI-based continuations beside nine human-written (Study 1, N=120) or nine original continuations (Study 2, N=302) and decided "whether a continuation was written with an AI-tool or not". The readers "generally had low accuracy for differentiating between text types but were overconfident in their decisions", and rated the AI continuations "less well-written, inspiring, fascinating, interesting, and aesthetic" than both the human-written and the original ones. The census record asks of the series how writers work with intelligent writing assistants and how readers judge text written with them, counts this result among what the series answers, and reads the study as meeting the question of its second anchor, AI Calls You Fake (#1722), "directly". That essay sets four independent questions about a work, whether its maker exists, whether the work happened, whether it is true and what kind of work it is, and names as the existence tax the move that spends evidence about one of them as an answer to another. The archive's papers set the human/AI binary against the conditions of writing: the pristine fallacy classifies text by its writer's identity, human or machine, since "'human-written' describes the author, not the distribution" (#856); the binary of "human-written" and "AI-generated" elides structured collaborative practice (#666); and the Reverse Turing Test keeps the detection of purely AI-generated against purely human-written text apart from its Mediation Index, which sorts human writing with AI mediation from human writing without it (#161). The Certified Center reads a journal's AI-authorship policy as making human-authorship provenance decisive and handing the question "machine-generated?" to a machine classifier, and proposes that under detector enforcement "'100% human' becomes the most machine-determined property of the text". The Reverse Turing Test proposes, on three lines of evidence on AI-assisted writing, that the human/synthetic binary is no longer reliable and that mediation signatures may pass into a writer's unaided practice through habituation, and The Wolf Boy reads the AI-habituated writer as on the path of capacity collapse. The archive's erratum of 5 September 2026 records that ground as "a hypothesis with a specified test, not a result", and states the published finding on essays co-written with a model at its limit: the reduced diversity was attributed "to the model-contributed text; the human-contributed text was unaffected in that design". The Anthology links pages on names, ORCID iDs and verified authors, which the census did not save, so how the record holds a name variant or pseudonym is not recorded. Wikipedia has no article on the series under either name, no redirect to one, and no article-space page carrying either name. Asked "In2Writing workshop" on 1 November 2026, signed out, Google's AI Overview gave the series by its purpose, its third and fourth editions and its website; the Capture Registry finds the first workshop and its reader study not carried, the second and third workshops outside the census record, no editor named, and the venue identifier only on a card. The census holds the series as an empirical comparator in its areas of machine co-authorship and reception research, under its organizing question, "How is authorship made, named, distributed, attributed and sustained across persons, personas, collectives and machine participation, and what is lost when those relations are collapsed?", and admits it by its rule that a row is "a resource that gathers and holds many other works or records and says what it holds"; its negative tags keep the row apart from the Anthology as a whole, from records of literary works and from policy venues on AI authorship, and mark the run on the saved evidence as incomplete.

v0.10 §0.5: the first diff is ontological and narrow. T and the field agree on the entity (a workshop series on intelligent and interactive writing assistants, by its name and purpose). What T keeps of its own six cards is the past: two editions read off card 2 and cards 3 and 4, both carried as "Past Events". What it leaves is the series' present and its persons: the fifth workshop, which the card T itself gives as the official website announces for the day after the capture, the editors on card 3's page, and the first workshop on card 5's own list. The composition's closer looks to "future editions" that card 1 already states, at a grain T does not compose.
